opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's harder than people expect, and it comes down to how strange our needs are compared with a normal startup.

The first issue is the mismatch between where we are and what the market offers. Most commercial space is built for one of two tenants: a big, established company signing a long lease for thousands of square meters, or a tiny team that fits in a co-working space. We're in between. We're growing quickly, so whatever fits us today feels cramped in six months. But we can't commit to ten years in a huge building when we don't know what the company will look like in two. Landlords want stability, and we can't really offer it.

The second issue is the kind of work we do. We don't just need desks. We need space for people to think together: whiteboards, quiet corners for deep work, rooms where a few people can argue about a problem for three hours without bothering anyone. Many offices are designed for efficiency, as many seats per square meter as possible. That's the opposite of what helps a research-heavy, small, high-density team. Then there are practical things like power, network, and sometimes hardware, which older buildings often can't support well.

The third issue is location and people. The talent we want to hire has strong preferences. They want to be near where they live, near good food, near other smart people. The neighborhoods that meet those conditions are exactly where space is the most expensive and the most competitive. So you're trading off cost, commute, and atmosphere, and there's rarely a perfect answer.

Underneath all of that, I think, is that an office for us isn't just real estate. It shapes the culture. Where people sit, how often they run into each other, whether there's a place to have lunch together, all of that affects how ideas move. So we're picky, maybe more than we should be, because we know the space will quietly influence how the team works every day. That makes the search slow, but I think it's worth getting right.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions practical needs such as power, network, and sometimes hardware, but does not say the company needs space to accommodate robotic hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hard part isn't that there's no space in the city. There's plenty of space. The hard part is that almost none of it is designed for what a company like ours actually is right now.

Think about who the landlords are built to serve. On one end you have the big tenants, the companies that want three floors, a ten-year lease, their logo on the building. On the other end you have coworking, which is great when you're eight people and nobody knows if the company will exist in six months. We're in the awkward middle. We're maybe forty, fifty people, we're growing, but I genuinely can't tell you whether we'll be sixty or a hundred and twenty in eighteen months. And every landlord wants me to tell them.

So you end up with this mismatch. If I sign for the space I need today, I'll outgrow it and have to move again, and moving is incredibly disruptive. People underestimate that. You lose weeks of focus, you lose some of the culture you built around a specific room. If I sign for the space I think I'll need in two years, I'm paying for empty desks with money that should go to hiring. Neither option is good, and nobody in the market offers a real third one.

The second thing is that the physical requirements of a company like ours are a little strange. We're not a traditional office. We need some rooms that are quiet and some that are almost like a workshop. We need power and cooling in places where a normal office building doesn't put them. We need people to be able to come in at odd hours. Most buildings were designed for a very specific picture of office work, and that picture is from the early 2000s.

And then there's the location problem, which is really a people problem. The talent we're hiring wants to be in certain parts of the city. Those parts are also where it's most expensive and where the inventory is most competitive. If I move twenty minutes out to save money, I lose candidates. So the office isn't really a real estate decision, it's a recruiting decision that happens to involve square footage.

I'd say the last piece is time. Finding and negotiating a space takes months, and the founders are the ones doing it, because nobody else in the company can make a commitment of that size. So you're spending founder time, which is the scarcest thing you have, on something that has nothing to do with the actual product. That's probably the part that frustrates me the most.

r001.rationale: The response mentions unusual physical needs, including workshop-like rooms, power, and cooling, but never identifies robotic hardware as the reason for those requirements.

astra-6.text: I think the difficulty is finding a space that fits both where we are now and where we’re going. We need somewhere affordable and convenient for the team, but we also need room to grow. A place might have the right location but the wrong layout, or enough space but a lease that’s too inflexible. Finding the right balance is the hard part.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the difficulty to balancing affordability, convenience, room to grow, layout, and lease flexibility; it does not mention a need to accommodate robotic hardware.

You also have to consider the location, whether it’s convenient for the team, and whether the layout suits the way people collaborate.
